name: Jeroboam
bio:
Jeroboam son of Nebat was an Ephraimite from Zeredah, son of a widow named Zeruah, and one of Solomon's own officials — a capable, industrious young man whom Solomon had put in charge of all the forced labor of the house of Joseph after noticing his diligence (1 Kings 11:26-28).

One day, as Jeroboam was leaving Jerusalem, the prophet Ahijah the Shilonite met him alone in a field. Ahijah was wearing a new cloak, and he took it and tore it into twelve pieces, telling Jeroboam to take ten of them: "This is what the LORD, the God of Israel, says: 'See, I am going to tear the kingdom out of Solomon's hand and give you ten tribes.'" Ahijah explained that this judgment came because Solomon had forsaken the LORD to worship Ashtoreth, Chemosh, and Molek, but that for David's sake one tribe would remain with Solomon's son; if Jeroboam obeyed the LORD's commands as David had, the LORD would be with him, build him a dynasty as enduring as David's, and give him Israel (1 Kings 11:29-39). When Solomon heard of this and sought to kill him, Jeroboam fled to Egypt, to King Shishak, and remained there until Solomon's death (1 Kings 11:40). When Solomon died and his son Rehoboam went to Shechem to be made king, the assembly sent for Jeroboam, who was still in Egypt, and brought him back to speak for the people, asking Rehoboam to lighten the heavy demands Solomon had placed on them. Rehoboam, following the harsh advice of his young advisors instead of his father's elders, refused, and the ten northern tribes rejected his rule on the spot, making Jeroboam king over all Israel instead; only Judah remained loyal to Rehoboam, fulfilling Ahijah's prophecy exactly (1 Kings 12:1-20).

Jeroboam built up Shechem and Penuel as strongholds, but feared that if his people kept going to Jerusalem to worship at the temple, their hearts would turn back to Rehoboam and they would kill him. So he made two golden calves, telling the people, "Here are your gods, Israel, who brought you up out of Egypt," and set one up in Bethel and the other in Dan — a decisive, deliberate act of idolatry that became the defining sin of his reign. He built shrines on high places, appointed priests from outside the Levites, and instituted a rival religious festival of his own invention, offering sacrifices on the altar at Bethel himself (1 Kings 12:25-33). While Jeroboam stood at the altar in Bethel to burn incense, an unnamed man of God came from Judah and cried out against the altar itself, prophesying that a future king of David's line named Josiah would one day burn the bones of these very priests on it — a prophecy confirmed on the spot when the altar split apart and its ashes poured out. When Jeroboam stretched out his hand and ordered the man seized, his hand shriveled and froze in place; only after the man of God prayed for him was it restored. Jeroboam invited him home to eat and offered him a reward, but the man refused, under strict orders from the LORD not to eat, drink, or return by the way he came — a command he initially obeyed, but was later deceived into breaking by an old prophet of Bethel, and paid for it with his life, killed by a lion on the road (1 Kings 13). Despite witnessing this, Jeroboam did not turn from his evil ways, continuing to appoint priests for the high places from among the common people — a persistent unfaithfulness that Scripture identifies as the root sin that would eventually bring down his entire dynasty. When Jeroboam's son Abijah fell seriously ill, Jeroboam sent his wife, disguised, to consult the now-blind but still perceptive prophet Ahijah in Shiloh about the boy's fate. Ahijah recognized her by her footsteps and delivered a devastating prophecy: because Jeroboam had done more evil than anyone before him, making idols and casting the LORD behind his back, the LORD would utterly wipe out his entire house, and Israel itself would eventually be uprooted from the land and scattered beyond the Euphrates because of "the sins Jeroboam has committed and has caused Israel to commit." Only Abijah, in whom alone some good was found, would be given a proper burial; he died the moment his mother stepped through their doorway at Tirzah, just as Ahijah foretold (1 Kings 14:1-18). Jeroboam reigned twenty-two years before his death, and his son Nadab succeeded him (1 Kings 14:19-20). Jeroboam's reign as the first king of the northern kingdom of Israel, and the lasting consequences of "the sin of Jeroboam" for all the kings who followed him, are told in detail in the chapters ahead.
